sections.title: Origins & History
sections.text: Nalanda, in Bihar, was one of the world's first great residential universities, and its ruins are among the most important sites of ancient Indian learning. The Nalanda Mahavihara flourished from about the 5th century CE, with royal patronage beginning under the Gupta ruler Kumaragupta I, and continued until about the 12th century. At its height, it is said to have attracted thousands of students and teachers from India and across Asia, including China, Korea, Japan, Tibet and Southeast Asia. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang studied and stayed here in the 7th century and left a detailed description, and another Chinese monk, Yijing, also visited.

sections.title: Beauty & Atmosphere
sections.text: The beauty of the site lies in its order and its red brick architecture. The excavated area shows a series of monasteries built around courtyards, with rows of small cells for monks, each with a stone bed and alcove. Large temples and stupas, such as Temple No. 3, rise in terraces with stucco figures and steps, and a long north-south axis of monasteries and shrines gives the site a clear plan. Sprawling lawns surround the remains, making a calm, open setting.

sections.title: Architecture & Highlights
sections.text: Students studied Buddhist philosophy as well as logic, grammar, medicine, mathematics and astronomy, and the great library, said to have been housed in several multi-storey buildings, was famous. Debates and discussions were an important part of learning. The institution was damaged and abandoned after attacks around 1193, and later disappeared from view, until the ruins were identified in the 19th century and excavated in the 20th century by the Archaeological Survey of India.

sections.title: Famous For
sections.text: Nalanda was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016. It is famous as a symbol of knowledge and international exchange, and a modern Nalanda University was established nearby in the 21st century to revive its spirit.

visitor_tips: Visitors can explore the ruins and the small Archaeological Museum in about two to three hours, preferably in the cooler months from October to March.
A guide helps to explain the layout.
Rajgir, with its ancient sites and hot springs, Pawapuri and Bodh Gaya are close by.
